segments.narration: Snow fell across North America in June. A strange dry fog dimmed the sky, turning the sun blood-red.
In 1816, crops froze overnight and mass starvation broke out across two continents.
Terrified families burned furniture for heat in August. What if summer was gone forever?
The culprit sat half a world away in Indonesia. Mount Tambora had erupted, launching nearly nine cubic miles of volcanic material into the atmosphere.

accuracy_flags.claim: Snow fell across parts of North America during the month of July in 1816.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference article states that snow fell in North America in June (such as June 6 in Albany, New York, and Dennysville, Maine). July saw severe cold, frost, and ice, but not recorded snowfall.

accuracy_flags.claim: The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia ejected roughly thirty-six cubic miles of material.
accuracy_flags.note: The article states that Mount Tambora ejected at least 37 cubic kilometers (8.9 cubic miles) of dense-rock equivalent material, confusing cubic kilometers for cubic miles and describing the total mass as sulfur.
